content: Pulmonary hypertension is a medical condition that specifically affects the blood vessels in the lungs. It occurs when the blood pressure within the pulmonary arteries becomes abnormally elevated. This increased pressure forces the heart to work harder than usual to pump blood into the lungs, which can lead to damage to the heart over time. As a result, individuals with pulmonary hypertension may experience symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, and episodes of lightheadedness. In this condition, the walls of the blood vessels in the lungs develop an excessive amount of muscle, leading to narrowing of the arteries. Normally, the right ventricle of the heart pumps blood to the lungs at a relatively low pressure, as the distance the blood needs to travel is short. However, in pulmonary hypertension, the pressure in the pulmonary arteries becomes abnormally high. This narrowing of the arteries restricts blood flow, reducing the amount of oxygen that can be delivered to the blood. The early symptoms of pulmonary hypertension are often nonspecific and can mimic those of other medical conditions. These symptoms may include difficulty breathing and fatigue, which can delay diagnosis. As the disease progresses, more severe symptoms may develop, such as dizziness, chest pain, swelling in the ankles, and a sensation of the heart racing or pounding (palpitations). Pulmonary hypertension can occur at any age, including in children, but its prevalence increases with age. It is more commonly observed in women, non-Hispanic Black individuals, and people aged 75 years or older. There are several underlying causes of pulmonary hypertension. These include high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries due to congenital heart defects, connective tissue diseases, coronary artery disease, systemic hypertension, liver disease (such as cirrhosis), blood clots in the lungs, and chronic lung diseases like emphysema. Genetic factors also play a role in the development of this condition. Pulmonary hypertension is often associated with other diseases, particularly lung and heart diseases, and heart failure is a frequent complication. Although not all cases of pulmonary hypertension can be prevented, certain measures can reduce the risk of developing the condition. These include adopting a healthy lifestyle and effectively managing conditions such as high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, chronic liver disease, and chronic lung diseases, particularly those caused by tobacco use. Currently, there is no cure for pulmonary hypertension. However, various treatment options are available to manage the condition and improve quality of life. These include medications that are inhaled, administered intravenously, or delivered under the skin. Diuretics may be prescribed to reduce swelling in the feet, and oxygen therapy can help improve oxygen levels in the blood.
